I. Listening comprehension (3 points)

   A CONVERSATION WITH YAYOI KUSAMA ON THE POWER OF ART AND
                         EMOTIONS

In this radio programme you are going to hear some new words. Read and listen to
them. Make sure you know what they mean.

art installations: instal·lacions artístiques – creacions artístiques / instalaciones
artísticas – creaciones artísticas

polka dots: estampat de topos / estampado de topos

boundless: sense límits / sin límites

tapestry: tapís / tapiz

Ready? Now read the questions on the following page. Read them carefully before
listening to the radio programme. [Now listen to the interview.]

Interviewer: In the realm of contemporary art, few figures are as iconic and enigmatic
as Yayoi Kusama. Renowned for her avant-garde art installations, polka dots, and
infinite reflections, Kusama has captivated the world with her unique artistic vision.
Today, we have the privilege of delving into the mind of this visionary artist, exploring
her thoughts on the transformative power of art. Good morning, thanks for being with
us today.

Yayoi Kusama: Good morning, thanks for the invitation.

Interviewer: Your art is often described as a celebration of love and hope. How do you
envision the relationship between your work and these powerful emotions?

Yayoi Kusama: Love and hope are the essence of my art. They are the driving forces
behind my creations. When people encounter my installations, I want them to feel a
sense of boundless love and hope, transcending the boundaries of time and space.
Through my work, I aim to cultivate a shared experience that unites people in a
profound, positive way.

Interviewer: That was deep indeed! Your "Infinity Rooms" are immersive experiences
that transport viewers into realms beyond this world. How do these installations
contribute to the exploration of love and hope?

Yayoi Kusama: The "Infinity Rooms" are like cosmic vessels, offering a glimpse into
the countless possibilities of love and hope. As visitors step into these spaces,
surrounded by endless reflections, they are immersed in a universe of boundless
                                                                      Pàgina 2 de 5
                                                                       Anglès
Proves d’accés a la Universitat 2026, convocatòria ordinària. Criteri específic d'avaluació


potential. It's a symbolic journey that mirrors the limitless nature of love and hope,
inviting individuals to reflect on their own place within the cosmic tapestry. I believe
sharing these positive emotions is the power of art. I fight anxiety and fear every day,
and the only method I have found that relieves my illness is to keep creating this type
of art.

Interviewer: Actually, in your autobiography, you mention struggling with mental health
issues. How has art been a source of healing and hope for you?

Yayoi Kusama: Art has been my refuge, a sanctuary where I can channel my
innermost feelings. In the darkest moments of my mental health struggles, creating art
became a lifeline. It allowed me to transform pain into beauty, despair into hope. Art
has been a cathartic journey, helping me to navigate the complexities of my emotions.

Interviewer: In any case, your use of polka dots is a signature element in your art. I
perceive these motifs as a representation of hallucinatory visions. Similar to how
episodes of depersonalization invoke fear, these dots create a visual manifestation of
anxiety. The dots multiply and attach themselves to the surroundings, becoming a form
of psychic obsession that you attempt to run away from.

Yayoi Kusama: Yes, I paint them abundantly; it's my way of trying to escape.

Interviewer: But can you also tell us about the significance of polka dots in conveying
positive messages?

Yayoi Kusama: Polka dots are a symbol of the world, the cosmos, and our
interconnectedness. When I cover surfaces with dots, I'm expressing the idea that we
are all dots in this vast universe. The repetition of dots signifies the multiplicity of
individuals, yet the pattern also reflects unity. It's a visual metaphor for the collective
energy that binds us together, creating a sense of harmony and love.

Interviewer: Oh wow. Now, your installations are experienced by people from diverse
backgrounds. How do you believe your art can bridge cultural gaps and speak a
universal language of love and hope?

Yayoi Kusama: Art transcends cultural barriers, you know, it's a universal language
that speaks directly to the heart. My installations are intentionally designed to be
inclusive, offering a space where people from all walks of life can connect on a
fundamental level. Love and hope, being universal emotions, provide a common
ground for individuals to come together, fostering a sense of unity that surpasses
cultural differences.

Interviewer: Can you tell us about your time in Japan before going to the US? You
moved to New York at twenty-seven. By then, you must have already developed your
unique style as a painter, rooted in Japan. Yet you didn’t emphasize your identity as a
Japanese artist.
                                                                      Pàgina 3 de 5
                                                                       Anglès

Yayoi Kusama: I wasn't really aware of it. In Japan, the art community isolated me
because of my mental health struggles. That's why I chose to leave Japan and pursue
my art in New York. I picked America because of my connections and the belief that
the future of art was in New York. However, I faced challenges due to restrictions on
foreign exchange imposed by the Japanese government. I even had to sell my
kimonos.

Interviewer: How do you see the role of art evolving in society, especially in fostering a
sense of hope and unity in the face of global challenges?

Yayoi Kusama: In times of uncertainty, art becomes a ray of light. It has the power to
inspire, uplift, and unite communities. As we confront global challenges, art catalyzes
change, encouraging collective action and fostering a shared vision of a better future.
It's a testament to the enduring capacity of art to instill hope and bring people together
in the pursuit of a brighter tomorrow.

Interviewer: This interview has come to a close, leaving us with a profound
understanding of how this visionary artist continues to shape the landscape of
contemporary art with her timeless messages of love and hope.

Reading · PAU 2026 · Juny (TEI) · Sèrie 5

    Part 2: Reading comprehension

           THE SCIENCE OF FEAR: HOW IT AFFECTS YOUR BODY AND MIND
         Fear is a natural response that has helped humans survive dangerous situations for centuries.
         While, unlike those faced by our ancestors, today’s threats are less likely to involve sabre-tooth
           tigers, haunted houses, scary movies, and harmless pranks still trigger the same physical and
         emotional reactions. The body’s fight-or-flight response releases stress hormones and prepares
     5  us to either face the challenge or escape it. But how exactly does fear work, and what happens
       when it is activated too often?
           The amygdala is a part of the brain that handles the processing of emotions and detection
          of danger. The fear response originates from it; upon detecting an apparent peril, signals are
          sent to the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus is an organ that initiates nervous and endocrine
    10  systems. Further, it encourages the release of stress hormones like cortisol, adrenaline, and
          noradrenaline. These chemicals cause a chain reaction in the body: your heart beats faster to
       pump oxygen-rich blood to your muscles and brain, your breathing quickens, your pupils dilate
          for better vision, and your muscles tense up ready for action. Adrenaline also reduces pain and
         heightens focus, allowing you to respond effectively to a threat. Interestingly, the release of
    15  dopamine, another hormone, can create a feeling of happiness during fear-inducing situations,
        which explains why some people enjoy being scared.
           Your brain doesn’t instantly distinguish between actual and imagined dangers. When
        an actor in a haunted house jumps out wearing a scary mask, for example, your body
         automatically behaves as if the danger were real. This is the automatic and brief initial phase
    20  of the fear response. However, the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain that is responsible for
          reasoning, quickly weighs this event. It confers with the hippocampus, an organ that retrieves
          the memories of similar events from storage to determine if there really is any danger. If you
        have been through a haunted house before, your brain knows the threat is not real, and the fear
         response turns off. But when the situation is unfamiliar—say, some terrifying scene in a horror
    25  movie—your body may release stress hormones, and physical effects—such as a racing heart or
         sweaty palms—may be more obvious.
            While the fear response is necessary for survival, frequent activation can damage the
         body. Continuous release of stress hormones may lead to high blood pressure, heart problems,
          digestive issues and immune system dysregulation because your body is constantly in “high
    30   alert” mode. Chronic exposure to jump scares can also desensitize the brain to real threats,
          potentially dulling critical survival instincts.
          Some groups should take more care with scary activities. For instance, people with heart
          diseases, chronic pain, and anxiety disorders are more sensitive to the negative side effects of
          scares. According to experts, scary activities are not recommended in order to protect mental
    35  and physical health.
              Controlled scares—the ones in haunted houses or elsewhere—are enjoyable to many. The
         temporary flash of stress hormones followed by relief creates an exhilarating sensation. But
           just like with any other activity involving health risks, moderation must be observed. When you
        become aware of what fear is, you can appreciate its role in survival and entertainment but also
    40   treat its impact on your health with respect.

                                                                         Text adapted from an article by
                                              Daryl Austin. National Geographic [online] (October 2, 2024)
